findings.claim: Homer’s Iliad, Book 3 (lines 121–244), is presented as the prescribed Helen passage.
findings.truth: The prescribed Homer passage is Iliad 3:121–180, not 121–244.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/classical-civilisation-J199.md, Women in the Ancient World prescribed literary sources, p. 15

findings.claim: The answer to what Tarpeia received in exchange and what happened to her gives only her death.
findings.truth: Tarpeia demanded what the Sabines wore on their arms; they crushed her with their shields.
findings.evidence: Livy, History of Rome 1.11; source context is required by the specification’s Tarpeia topic

findings.claim: The bride dedicated her kalyptra, then the groom lifted it in the wedding ritual.
findings.truth: Offerings before marriage included childhood toys and often a lock of hair. The kalyptra was the veil worn for the unveiling ritual, not an offering described in the fetched wedding source.
findings.evidence: Archaiologia Online, The wedding ceremony in ancient Greece; fetched source identifies the hair offering to Artemis and the unveiling ritual

findings.claim: Spartan women could own property and speak publicly; Athenian women could not.
findings.truth: Athenian women could hold and inherit property, although a kyrios generally managed it and their control was more limited. Spartan women had wider property rights.
findings.evidence: Perseus, Thomas R. Martin, Property, Social Freedom, and Athenian Women; specification p. 13 requires comparison of legal rights and property ownership

findings.claim: Syssitia are men’s communal barracks where husbands slept.
findings.truth: Syssitia were compulsory communal meals or dining groups for Spartan male citizens. Plutarch describes younger husbands returning to sleep with other young men, not sleeping in a syssition.
findings.evidence: Plutarch, Lycurgus 15.3, fetched from Perseus; Oxford Classical Dictionary definition of agōgē context

findings.claim: The Hegeso Stele’s sculptor is unknown.
findings.truth: The specification identifies the Hegeso Stele as attributed to Callimachus.

findings.claim: The gynaikon was typically a fixed women’s section at the back or upper floor of an Athenian house.
findings.truth: Option 1: retain this as a literary ideal. Option 2: revise the lesson, glossary and questions to say that gynaikon could denote women’s household space, while archaeology does not establish a standard separate back or upper-floor women’s quarter.
findings.evidence: Oxford Academic, Household and City Organization at Olynthus; Cambridge, Domestic Comedy and the Classical Greek House; American School of Classical Studies at Athens, Women in the Athenian Agora
findings.ruling: Option 1 plus a caveat: literary ideal retained, one sentence notes archaeology shows no standard women's quarter.

findings.claim: “I hold here the dear child of my daughter, whom I held on my knees when we were alive and looked on the light of the sun; now dead, I hold it dead.”
findings.truth: The fetched Metropolitan Museum source gives a materially similar but differently worded translation of the Ampharete inscription. Do not replace this quotation without selecting and licensing a specific translation.
findings.evidence: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Fragments of the marble stele of a woman holding a baby

findings.claim: Athenian women entirely lacked property rights.
findings.truth: Athenian women could hold and inherit property, but a kyrios generally managed it and their control was more restricted than men’s or Spartan women’s.
findings.evidence: Perseus, Thomas R. Martin, Property, Social Freedom, and Athenian Women

findings.claim: Syssitia were communal dining and sleeping barracks, and a husband’s sleeping arrangement after marriage is identified as syssitia.
findings.truth: Syssitia were communal meals or dining groups. Younger husbands returned to communal quarters after visiting their wives; the two should not be equated.

findings.claim: “come back with your shield or on it” is presented as a Spartan saying.
findings.truth: The fetched Plutarch collection gives the saying as “Either this or upon this.” The lesson’s wording is a familiar paraphrase, not the fetched translation; retain no exact quotation unless a chosen translation is verified.
findings.evidence: Plutarch, Sayings of Spartan Women 16, fetched from University of Chicago Penelope

findings.claim: Patria potestas gave the paterfamilias legal authority over his wife, children and all household slaves.
findings.truth: Patria potestas concerned the paterfamilias’s children and descendants. A wife came under a husband’s manus only in a cum manu marriage; slavery was not patria potestas.
findings.evidence: Roman-law definitions of patria potestas and manus; specification p. 13 distinguishes cum manu and sine manu marriage

findings.claim: The so-called Sappho fresco depicts a wealthy, educated Roman woman and proves that education was part of the ideal for wealthy women.
findings.truth: Option 1: describe only the visible tablet and stylus, and say the subject’s identity is unknown. Option 2: present education as one interpretation, alongside scholarship that treats the figure as an idealised or Muse-like image rather than a portrait of a real educated woman.
findings.evidence: Smarthistory, Portrait of a Young Woman (known as Sappho); American Journal of Archaeology, Writing Paraphernalia, Tablets, and Muses in Campanian Wall Painting
findings.ruling: Option 2: one sentence presents education as one interpretation and notes the Muse/idealised reading.

summary: Five lessons were checked. Eleven verified issues have surgical edits; two interpretation issues require editorial judgement, and two quotations are recorded without replacement.
